title: Deterministic Calculation Engine
markdown:
The **calc** module (`openexecutive.calc`) is the deterministic calculation
subsystem: typed contracts, a closed unit registry, an explicit authority
boundary, and — as of Phase 2 — a standalone execution engine with
engine-owned fingerprints. Phase 3B1 added a caller: two modules under
`specialists/` that turn a specialist's proposed arithmetic into engine-executed
records. They are the only production importers of this package.

The gateway is **deliberately unwired** — nothing constructs it. Putting
unconsumed work on the live CFO path would be cost and risk for no benefit, so
the CFO, Executive, Committee, UI and persistence are untouched. That is
Phase 3B2.

Phase 1 shipped the contracts alone, deliberately, so the engine would be
written against a boundary already reviewed rather than one it invented while
implementing. Phase 2 supplied the executor.

### Three types, three owners

The authority story is which type can carry what.

| Type | Owner | Can a model write it? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CalculationProposal` | model-shaped, application-validated | yes — it has nowhere to put an answer |
| `CalculationRequest` | the gateway | no — it never sees a model-supplied id |
| `CalculationResult` | the engine, via one factory | no |

A proposal carries intent only: no request id, no correlation, no result,
status, evidence, fingerprint, authority stamp or timestamp. Because the model
is `extra="forbid"`, a payload attempting any of them is rejected loudly rather
than stripped quietly — the attempt stays visible.

The record the gateway returns is a frozen **dataclass** — a transport
container, and nothing more. It establishes **no provenance at all**: direct
construction, pickle, pydantic's own dataclass handling, persistence and replay
all reconstitute one, and none of them attests to where its contents came from.

Two successive versions of this document claimed otherwise and both were wrong —
first that there was "no deserialization path", then that there was "no
*automatic*" one. Pydantic builds validators for stdlib dataclasses, so a model
field of this type will happily deserialize an untrusted body.

Trust in the records comes from one place: the gateway obtained them from the
engine, in this process. Anything that receives this type from elsewhere has
learned nothing and must re-establish provenance by its own means.

That distinction is the whole reason the field does not live on the
model-authored result type instead. *That* type is auto-deserialized, and an
earlier design putting a calculation record on it allowed a hand-written
`1 + 1 = 999999` to arrive through an ordinary payload wearing a real authority
stamp.

### Identifiers the model cannot choose

Every request id is minted from a domain tag, the case and run, the specialist,
the proposal's position, its validated claim reference, and the proposal's
canonical content — each component length-prefixed before hashing, so no two
distinct component tuples can share a pre-image.

The same care applies to *who may execute at all*. Three tests bound that set —
two allowlists plus the gateway suite's own one-door re-assertion — and all
three share one import resolver, because separate copies drifted and between
them missed five ordinary import forms, including `from openexecutive import
calc`, which reaches the engine without ever naming it, since the package
re-exports the execution functions. Reaching is therefore defined over the
execution surface rather than a module name; importing a calculation *type* is
explicitly not reaching. Each form is driven through each real scan over a
temporary tree, so a regression fails in the suite rather than in review.

The resolver's scope is stated, not implied. Directory filters are matched
relative to the scan root, so a checkout that happens to live under a directory
named `tests` or `calc` is still scanned rather than silently skipped. Dynamic
imports are resolved only when the module name is a string literal passed to
`importlib.import_module`, a bare `import_module`, or `__import__`; a computed
name, an aliased `importlib`, or a module reached through a dependency is not
statically decidable and is controlled by review, and a test pins that boundary
so the documentation cannot outrun the check.

It is deterministic in exactly those inputs: no clock, no counter, no salt, so a
replay produces byte-identical ids. The specialist is inside the derivation, so
two specialists proposing the *same* arithmetic get different addresses while
their fingerprints still match — the calculation is identical, the records stay
separately traceable.

### Unsafe text is refused, never rewritten

Two screens, not one, and neither ever rewrites anything.

Both share a base rule — a string must be non-empty, within its field's length
bound, and printable. Python's `str.isprintable()` carries the character check:
it is false for every Unicode *Other* or *Separator* character except the ASCII
space, so line feeds, NEL, U+2028/9, escapes, the bidirectional overrides,
surrogates and unassigned codepoints are all refused. Because the rule is
defined by category rather than by a list someone maintains, a character added
to Unicode later is covered too.

Rejection rather than sanitisation is a correction learned the hard way. A
rewriting version rewrote the specialist parser's own segment delimiter and
showed operators four substitution markers — the documented signal for *"an
unsafe character was removed here"* — in a record where nothing hostile had ever
appeared. Rewriting also makes a record say something the specialist did not.
Refusing costs one proposal, reports a bounded code, and leaves every surviving
string exactly as authored.

### One bad proposal costs one slot

A reference to a claim nobody made, or a request that will not construct, drops
that proposal alone; its siblings still execute. An engine failure returns one
typed *unavailable* record per request rather than nothing, so a reader can tell
a calculation nobody asked for from one that could not run.

No evidence is passed, because no resolver exists yet — every record honestly
reports that its inputs are unverified, and correct arithmetic over unbacked
numbers is still unbacked.

An unusable timestamp is handed to the engine **unaltered**, so it comes back as
the engine's own typed rejection rather than being quietly replaced. An earlier
version substituted a fallback first, which meant a refused clock returned a
*verified* result stamped 1 January 1970 with nothing recording the swap — a
fabricated instant in a record whose entire purpose is to say what actually
happened.

### Where the two screens differ

Identifiers — a claim reference, an operand id — are *matched*, so they carry
one extra rule: no surrounding whitespace. `"c1"` and `" c1"` must not be two
spellings of one thing, because a validator that trims turns an equality check
into a near-equality check.

Descriptive text — a purpose, a label, a quoted excerpt — is only read, so it
gets the base rule and nothing more. Semicolons included: an earlier version
refused those because a different module joins its own messages with one, which
rejected a specialist writing "runway; then covenant headroom" for a reason
having nothing to do with its field. Escaping a delimiter belongs to whatever
renders it, not to whatever accepts it.

Multi-line quotations are refused rather than flattened. Preserving line
structure needs a quotation contract — how an excerpt is bounded, escaped and
rendered — that this slice does not have, and a rejected quote is honest where a
silently flattened one is not.

### Why it exists

A controlled, single-specialist evaluation measured the CFO on three
reconciliation checks with all required evidence verified present in its
context. It scored 0/5, 1/5 and 0/5. The failure was specific and repeatable:
the model identified the correct operands and the correct formula — `52 kg/m²`,
`11 ha = 110,000 m²`, "yield per m² × area" — and then returned a result off by
a factor of ten. A second calculation came back carrying the literal placeholder
`XX` where a number belonged. A follow-up experiment that added a mandatory
"show your arithmetic" protocol to the CFO prompt was measured and **rejected**:
it suppressed placeholders and stopped the model using unverified figures as
covenant premises, but it also produced three *new* fabricated magnitudes. A
prompt can forbid a habit; it cannot install a capability.

The conclusion the contracts encode: **execution moves somewhere deterministic,
and the record must distinguish four things the old string boundary could not** —
what the model proposed, what an engine computed, whether the inputs were backed
by evidence, and whether the computed figure conflicts with what the applicant
claimed. Those are four independent axes and the contract keeps them
independent.

### Ownership and dependencies

`calc` is a **leaf package**. It imports only `json`, `re`, `decimal`, `types`,
`typing`, `collections.abc`, `pydantic`, plus `hashlib` (the fingerprint digest,
confined to one module) and `time` (the engine's monotonic budget clock — never
a wall clock, and never the source of a record's timestamp, which the caller
supplies so tests can pin it). It must not import `agents`, `specialists`, `providers`,
`orchestrator`, `prompts`, `memory`, `api`, `workflows`, or `knowledge` — a test
asserts this. That constraint is what lets the future engine be tested with no
fixtures, no mocks, and no model. It has **no filesystem, network, or
code-execution authority**: AST tests run over every `.py` file found *on disk*
under the package directory, from a root anchored on the test file itself —
never on a module object, whose `__file__` the scanned code can rebind to point
the scanner at innocent bytes. The walk rejects any symlink under the package
and any importable non-source artifact (`.pyc`, `.so`), because a directory
without `__init__.py` is importable as a namespace package and a sourceless
`.pyc` never matches a `*.py` glob. It uses `os.walk` rather than a 3.13-only
`rglob` keyword, so it runs on the 3.11 the project actually ships. Relative imports are
resolved against the file's package, so `from .. import providers` is recorded
rather than skipped. Together they enforce an import allowlist and scan for
calls to `eval`, `exec`, `compile`, `open`, `subprocess`,
`importlib`, `socket`, `pickle` and their relatives. Their scope is stated
honestly in the tests — they catch direct imports and direct calls, not
indirection such as an aliased builtin or a mechanism reached through a
dependency, which are not statically decidable in general.

### The two status axes

`arithmetic_status` says whether an engine executed the expression.
`evidence.status` says whether the operands were backed. They are never merged,
because a result is routinely both correct and unsupported — recomputing an
applicant's own cost stack gives a right answer from numbers nobody has
corroborated. `ARITHMETIC_VERIFIED` combined with `UNSUPPORTED` is a legal,
tested state, and `is_verified_evidence()` is the single place the conjunction
is expressed, so a caller wanting the strong claim has to ask for it by name.
That claim is backed by a coherence validator on the evidence summary —
`ALL_SUPPORTED` is refused alongside any unbound operand *and* with an empty
bound list, an operand cannot be both bound and unbound, and the result
cross-checks every named id against the operands it actually records — so a
partial evidence layer that sets the status but not the bindings cannot forge
it. Every result-side *numeric* field is parsed through the same boundary as an
operand, so the literal placeholder `XX` cannot enter a value, a difference, a
ratio or a stated figure. It can still appear in prose fields — the executed
expression, a warning, an error detail — which are free text by design and are
bounded in length rather than in shape.

`CONFLICT_DETECTED` is deliberately **not** an arithmetic status. It lives on an
orthogonal `conflict` axis alongside `ORDER_OF_MAGNITUDE` — the class that
describes a stated 572 tonnes against a computed 5,720 — because a result is
frequently verified *and* conflicting, and one enum cannot carry both facts.

### Authority boundary

Stated separately per adversary, because the answers differ:

* **Against the model — structural.** A model speaks only through
  `CalculationRequest`. That type has no field for an arithmetic status, an
  evidence status, an authority stamp, a fingerprint, a timestamp, or a trusted
  source location, and every contract model is `extra="forbid"`, so a payload
  attempting one is *rejected* rather than silently stripped. There is no wire
  on which a model can assert its own arithmetic was checked. This is the same
  guarantee `specialists.result_contract` relies on for `verified_result`.
* **Against a same-process caller — conventional.** Python has no private
  constructor; `model_construct` and `object.__setattr__` bypass pydantic for
  any model. `issue_calculation_result()` is a single named, greppable channel
  that fills the authority stamp from a module constant rather than a caller
  argument. That is a convention with teeth, **not** a security boundary, and
  the module says so rather than overclaiming.

`SourceHint` is a narrow, deliberate non-reuse of `EvidenceRef`. `EvidenceRef`
carries `page`, `sheet`, `cell_range`, `url`, and `retrieved_at`, which are safe
there only because one function strips them from model output; the *type*
permits them. Embedding it in a model-authored request would let any other
deserialization path carry a model-asserted spreadsheet cell through as
confirmed provenance. `SourceHint` simply has no field in which to assert one,
and its `retrieval_id_hint` is named for what it is.

### Units and numbers

The registry is closed and exact. `pct` and `pct_point` are different
*dimensions*, so comparing a margin against a percentage-point gap is a type
error rather than a judgement call. What this phase enforces on the record is the
part that needs no operation semantics: a single operand's `original_unit →
normalized_unit` step must be a conversion that could actually happen, and a
month↔year step must state its basis. Per-operation dimensional signatures are
deliberately left to the engine — a draft encoded them here and rejected the
package's own motivating calculation, `5,720,000 kg ÷ 110,000 m² = 52 kg/m²`. `ha → m²` is exactly 10,000 and `t → kg`
exactly 1,000, held as `Decimal`, so no conversion the engine performs can carry
error originating here. `month ↔ year` shares a dimension but is marked
`explicit_required`: a month is not 1/12 of a financial year under every
day-count basis, and annualising without saying how is the failure the contract
exists to catch. Currency is written `currency:XXX` with an ISO-shaped code —
never a bare `TND` — and `additively_compatible` refuses a cross-currency pair,
because Version 1 ships no exchange-rate authority. That predicate is the
vocabulary the engine applies; this phase enforces it on an operand's own
normalisation step, not across an operation's operands.

Floats are rejected at the boundary with an explicit error, never coerced.
Ambiguous separators are rejected rather than guessed: `1,234` fails under the
plain format, comma-thousands must be asked for by name, and decimal commas are
unsupported rather than supported-and-ambiguous. NaN, Infinity, out-of-range
exponents, and over-long literals all fail closed — the exponent bound applying
to zero as well, since `0e-2000000000` compares equal to zero yet formats
positionally into a two-billion-character string. Nothing scales thousands into
millions.

### The engine

`engine.py` executes exactly twelve operations, dispatched from a closed
mapping — never looked up from model text, and with no expression parser
anywhere. `execute()` and `execute_batch()` **always** return a typed
`CalculationResult`: no exception caused by request data escapes them. Their
signatures accept no fingerprint, no arithmetic status, no authority stamp, no
engine version, and no pre-executed expression; every one of those is
constructed internally.

Arithmetic is `Decimal` only, inside a `localcontext()` at 50-digit precision —
which is what finally makes Phase 1's declared `MAX_PRECISION_REQUEST`
non-inert. `InvalidOperation`, `DivisionByZero`, `Overflow` and
`FloatOperation` are trapped so they surface as typed statuses instead of
propagating NaN; `Inexact`, `Rounded`, `Subnormal`, `Underflow` and `Clamped`
are not, since they are the normal condition of division. All nine signals are
pinned explicitly, and the context is built from scratch rather than copied from
the caller's — a bare `localcontext()` inherits ambient rounding and traps, which
once split fingerprints and denied service process-wide.

Intermediates run at full precision and the caller-visible rounding happens once,
at the final boundary, with both the exact and the rounded value recorded. That
is not the only rounding: each operand is normalised to its target unit first, so
a division-based conversion rounds there too — the divergence sits at digit 50,
far below the reported scale.

Multiplicative operands are normalised onto their dimension's base unit before
they are combined, and the target must be that base. Validating by dimension
alone accepted `52 kg/m² × 11 ha → kg` and returned **572** — the exact 10⁴
error this package exists to prevent, arriving with a verified status. The two
motivating calculations work in both directions and from un-normalised inputs:
`52 kg/m² × 11 ha = 5,720,000 kg` and `5,720,000 kg ÷ 110,000 m² = 52 kg/m²`. A Phase 1 draft rejected the second as
a dimension mismatch, which is exactly why operation semantics live in the
engine and not in the contract.

### Fingerprints

Canonical JSON then SHA-256, computed by the engine **after** validation and
normalisation. Identity includes the schema version, engine authority and
version, operation, ordered normalised operands and their units, target unit,
scale, rounding, the applicant's stated value, and any operation-specific
policy; it excludes request, case, run, specialist and claim ids, timestamps,
labels and purpose prose. Verified stable across processes and across
`PYTHONHASHSEED` values.

A failed calculation carries **no** fingerprint. That is a documented rule, not
an oversight: a calculation that did not run has no identity, and minting one
would let a deduplication index answer "already computed" for something never
computed.

### Batching and budgets

Evidence is scoped per request — there is no batch-wide parameter, because
`operand_id` is unique only *within* a request and a shared summary stamped
validated evidence onto siblings whose ids happened to collide. At most 32
requests, one typed result each, in request order. A failure does not
erase its siblings — Phase 1 measured the alternative, where a single malformed
claim discarded all eleven in a specialist result. Wall-clock budgets are
measured with a monotonic clock and are **reported, not preemptive**: a
synchronous Python call cannot interrupt itself without threads or signals,
which this package deliberately does not own. The real protection is that size
and exponent limits are enforced before any `Decimal` work, so no authorised
operation has a cost superlinear in its input length.

### Version 1 scope

Twelve declared operations: add, subtract, multiply, divide, sum_components,
percentage_of, percentage_point_difference, ratio, weighted_average, variance,
convert_unit, interval_implied_total. IRR, XIRR, NPV, CAGR, debt schedules and
sensitivity tables are **absent on purpose** — each needs a cash-flow *series*
contract (timing, periodicity, day count) that this scalar operand model does
not carry, and none is needed by the measured failures.

A closed typed-operation API was chosen over a parsed expression grammar. A
grammar buys arbitrary formulas, which Version 1 does not want, in exchange for
the only meaningful code-execution surface in the system.
